query: Which material can be used for superconducting properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy that is specifically enriched with niobium (Nb) may exhibit measurable superconducting properties at cryogenic temperatures, owing to the inherent superconductivity of Nb and the potential for high-entropy disorder to favor electron pairing.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast or additively manufactured refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) in a predominantly single-phase BCC or FCC structure without engineered superconducting behavior.
generation.intervention: Increase the Nb content in the HEA (e.g., using an alloy system such as NbTaTiZr) and apply controlled thermal treatments to achieve homogeneous microstructure and minimize phase decomposition.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed at cryogenic temperatures, under conditions with minimal magnetic field interference.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform distribution of Nb atoms within the high‐entropy matrix that maintains a stable, single-phase microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The superconductivity is hypothesized to be due to niobium’s known ability to support Cooper pair formation, with the HEA’s compositional complexity and disorder possibly modifying electron scattering and density of states to enable a superconducting transition under cryogenic conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: At sufficiently low temperatures, the Nb-enriched HEA will exhibit a distinct superconducting transition (zero electrical resistance and characteristic magnetic susceptibility features) compared to a baseline HEA with lower Nb content.
generation.baseline: A similar refractory HEA having a lower fraction of Nb (or lacking targeted Nb enrichment) that does not exhibit superconductivity under the same cryogenic conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect hinges on maintaining the single-phase stability of the HEA; phase decomposition or formation of competing phases upon thermal treatment, as sometimes observed in HEAs, may limit the superconducting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While Nb is a known elemental superconductor, it remains uncertain to what extent the disorder inherent in HEAs will enhance or suppress the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and other related parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEAs, one enriched in Nb (e.g., a NbTaTiZr-based alloy) and one baseline alloy with lower Nb content. Process both sets under identical casting or additive manufacturing conditions and apply the same controlled thermal treatments. Cool the samples to cryogenic temperatures while monitoring electrical resistance and magnetic susceptibility.
measurements: Measurement of the superconducting critical temperature (Tc) via four-point probe resistance tests
Detection of zero electrical resistance below Tc
Magnetization measurements (e.g., Meissner effect via SQUID magnetometry)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-enriched HEA does not show a lower temperature transition with zero resistance and distinct magnetic signatures compared to the baseline, or if both sets of alloys behave identically (i.e. no superconducting transition is observed), then the hypothesis is falsified.
